It's not an apples to apples comparison. If you took fifty male executives and fifty of their female secretaries and compared them, then of course you'd get a huge gap. But it's not because the secretaries suffer from discrimination; it's because they have lower paying jobs.

In general, women tend to pursue lower-paying jobs and careers. At the low end, they'd rather be a cashier than do physically demanding work. At the middle to upper end, they prefer easier careers with more work/life flexibility, benefits, and creature comforts, and they're more likely to take time off to have kids or simply retire after a decade in the field and become homemakers depending on a male breadwinner.

That's on top of differences in education, hours worked, etc.

And when you get away from the aggregates, you find that gaps in different careers vary. Sometimes, there is a male bias in a given career. Sometimes, there is a female bias. To be clear: preventing clotting means getting a good fast draw (but don't use so much suction that you lyse red blood cells) and mixing in the anticoagulant as soon as possible and thoroughly. The chemicals do the magic. Rushing the blood to the laboratory will get the results that much faster, but won't affect the testing either way (with respect to clots).

Nearly all laboratory technicians (both medical laboratory scientists and medical laboratory technicians) have, at minimum, a couple of weeks of clinical phlebotomy experience. I performed over 500 blood draws during my training, although that's more than most (it was a busy clinic).

Many of us have either worked as phlebotomists or in laboratories or clinics where we're sometimes required to perform draws. We are familiar with infants, anxious children, irritable elderly patients, and those who _just won't bleed!_

Believe it or not, we are well aware that the specimens we're most likely to need again are the _hardest_ ones to obtain. If they were easy to collect, you would have received an acceptable specimen on the first attempt. It feels punitive and unreasonable to have to repeat the difficult draws when you did your best the first time. However, when treatment is guided by laboratory results, good patient care necessitates accurate data.

Use the largest needle you think you can get away with and place that needle cleanly in the center of the lumen of the vein. Don't use too much suction, don't draw too slowly either, and mix the blood with the anticoagulant as soon as possible, but don't mix by shaking the container violently (use several gentle full inversions). Do that and you should never get a hemolyzed sample, unless that's what the patient has.

If you read that and think, "but do you have any idea how hard it is to do it textbook-perfect every time!?", that's why the specimens keep hemolyzing. Yes, we do have an idea how hard it is, but the test doesn't care whether or not you gave it your best effort, it only measures what you produced - good or bad.
